analysis.one_liner: Gives unions equal access to workplaces and stiffens penalties when employers fire workers for organizing.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House committee with no cosponsors after a single member introduced it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change federal labor law in four ways: if a company holds meetings telling workers why they should reject a union, workers would get equal time, on the clock, to hear the union's side; unions would get access to worksites and company bulletin boards and mailboxes; workers fired for union activity could get triple back pay and sue for punitive damages; and if a new union and employer can't agree on a first contract, a mediator would be appointed and unresolved issues sent to binding arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize or already represented by a union. Today an employer can hold mandatory anti-union meetings with no union response allowed, can fire a union supporter and owe only back pay with no punitive damages, and can stall a first contract indefinitely. The bill would give the union equal presentation rights, make firing a union supporter expensive for the employer, and guarantee a first contract through arbitration.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers joining and represented by unions

how_it_helps.text: If an employer addresses employees on its premises or during work hours about union representation, workers must get an equal opportunity, without loss of time or pay, to hear the union's side in an equivalent manner.

Unions would have the right to enter areas where employees work, use the employer's bulletin boards and mailboxes, and use employer facilities for meetings, subject to reasonable National Labor Relations Board regulation.

When the labor board finds a worker was fired over an unfair labor practice, the employer would owe triple back pay, and the worker would be notified of the right to sue for punitive damages; the bill also makes firing a worker for protected organizing activity explicitly unlawful and lets workers sue in federal or state court for wrongful discharge damages.

If a newly certified union and employer cannot reach a first contract within 60 days, a mediator must be appointed, and either side can send unresolved issues to the Federal Mediation and Conciliation Service for binding arbitration 30 days later.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, especially non-union companies fighting organizing drives. They would share their facilities and communication channels with unions during campaigns, face triple back pay and lawsuit exposure when they fire workers illegally, and lose the ability to stall a first contract indefinitely once a union is certified.

drawbacks.text: The binding arbitration of first contracts removes bargaining flexibility from both sides: an arbitrator would write the terms of wages and conditions that the employer and the union could not agree on, a step critics of mandatory contract arbitration have long argued substitutes a third party's judgment for negotiated agreements.

Requiring unions to get equal presentation time and access to worksites when an employer holds meetings cuts against employers' rights to control their own property and speech during a union campaign, and the triple back pay and punitive-damages exposure would raise litigation costs for companies even in close cases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to a group with few legal protections today: under current law an employer can require workers to attend anti-union meetings with no union response, and an illegally fired organizer can wait years for back pay with no punitive damages. The costs fall on employers, in the form of union access to company property, treble damages, and an arbitrator writing first contracts. The heaviest design concern is mandatory binding arbitration of initial contracts, which takes final wage and terms decisions away from both the company and the union; the equal-access and penalty provisions track changes labor advocates have proposed to rebalance a process employers currently control.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced by one House member, sent to the Education and the Workforce Committee, passed to a subcommittee five weeks later, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jesse L. Jackson, Jr. introduced the Right to Organize Act of 2000 in the House on April 4, 2000.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the day it was introduced.
On May 17, 2000, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, where it stayed.
No other member cosponsored the bill, and the record shows no committee action, hearing, floor vote, or further movement before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers opposing stronger union-organizing rules are better off: they face no equal-access requirement, no treble back pay or punitive-damages exposure for firing organizers, and no binding arbitration of first contracts. Workers gained nothing, since the bill never advanced.

for.name: Rep. Jesse L. Jackson, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and offered it to the House; no other member joined as a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and never acted on it — no hearing, markup, or vote; its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee held it after May 17, 2000.

against.name: Rep. William Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled any action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll calls exist; it had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, making its level of support hard to read from the record alone.

industries.note: The bill would cost employers the ability to run one-sided anti-union meetings, expose them to triple back pay and punitive-damages suits when they fire organizers, and subject first contracts to binding arbitration. Its death in committee leaves current law in place, under which employers face far weaker penalties and unions have no guaranteed access to workers on company property.

The bill would entitle unions to equal presentation time, worksite access, and use of employer communication channels, and would give newly certified unions a guaranteed path to a first contract. Union organizing campaigns would become materially fairer for the workers they represent.
The bill would route first-contract mediation and binding arbitration through the service, expanding its role in resolving stalled negotiations.
